hints: Look closely at the clue about bases. If the sand rat PDx1 gene has much less A and T, what must it have much more of?
Remember how A-T pairs and G-C pairs differ in hydrogen bonds, and why sequencing needs single-stranded DNA to be kept apart.
walkthrough:
**Spot the base composition clue**

The question tells you the sand rat gene has a much lower proportion of A and T. That means it must have a much higher proportion of G and C.

Think: low AT = high GC.

**Link GC content to bond strength**

Now recall the pairing rules. A pairs with T by 2 hydrogen bonds, but G pairs with C by 3 hydrogen bonds.

$$ \text{A=T : 2 H-bonds, G} \equiv \text{C : 3 H-bonds} $$
So a GC-rich gene holds its two strands together much more strongly and is harder to keep as single strands for sequencing.

**Check statements 1 and 2**

Statement 1 is wrong because every diploid nucleus in one animal contains the same genome. An essential gene like PDx1 will be present in all nuclei, not just a few.

Statement 2 is also wrong because sequencing uses DNA, not mRNA. Whether a gene is transcribed in many cells or few cells does not change the DNA sequence you can extract and sequence.

**Conclude**

Only statement 3 explains the difficulty. Unusually strong hydrogen bonding from high GC content makes splitting off nucleotides one at a time very difficult.

options.A: Incorrect, as it includes 1 and 2 which are false. Gene presence and transcription pattern do not prevent DNA sequencing.
options.B: Incorrect, as statement 1 is false. All somatic nuclei contain the same genes, so the PDx1 gene is present in all nuclei.
options.C: Incorrect, as statement 2 is false. Transcription controls mRNA production, but DNA sequencing uses genomic DNA which is present regardless.
options.D: Correct, as only statement 3 is true. High GC content gives more triple hydrogen bonds, making strands hard to separate for sequencing.
